problem.title: Card-fraud scoring service
problem.context: A payments company scores every card transaction for fraud before it is authorized. It processes about 3,000 transactions per second on a normal day and up to five times as many during seasonal sales. Fraudsters adapt within weeks, and the confirmed fraud labels (chargebacks) arrive days to weeks after the transaction. Auditors and the card schemes can ask, months later, why a given transaction was scored the way it was. The ML team has five data scientists and two ML engineers. The company's operations team runs the data centres and the shared infrastructure, but there is no platform team for machine learning.

requirements.text: Score every card transaction before the authorization decision, using the cardholder's recent activity (for example, the spending of the last hour and the last day).
Update the model as new confirmed fraud cases arrive.
For any past score, show which model version and which input values produced it.
During a seasonal peak of 15,000 transactions per second, a score comes back within 30 ms at the 99th percentile.
When the scoring service or one of its data sources fails, authorizations go on. The business accepts weaker fraud detection for up to 15 minutes, but no authorization may fail because of scoring.
An auditor asks about a score from up to 13 months ago. Within one working day the team answers with the model version, the input values and the training data that model was built from.
When the fraud loss rate rises in one segment, a retrained model can be in production within 48 hours, after it has been compared with the current model on recent transactions.
Card data must stay inside the company's PCI-certified environment: no external service may process it.
Seven people build and run the system, with no dedicated ML platform team.

points.description: 1. Kafka-fed Flink aggregates activity in Redis, which six autoscaling Kubernetes replicas query through an XGBoost Python REST scorer. Requests time out after 25 ms to a rule-engine fallback; scores are audited for 13 months, while nightly Airflow training, MLflow lineage, shadow comparison, manual promotion, restart-time activation, feature explanations, and Grafana monitoring complete the lifecycle. 2. **Trade-off:** This provides low-latency scoring, fallback, auditability, controlled promotion, and operational visibility. It gives up immediate model activation, incurs on-premise retention and Kubernetes operations, and may let a nightly model trained on 90 days of labels lag changing fraud patterns.

values: Activity state: Kafka to Flink aggregates in Redis
points.description: Kafka streams card-activity events to Flink, which computes rolling aggregates such as transaction counts or spending totals. Flink writes the resulting activity state to Redis, where the fraud-scoring service can retrieve it with low latency. Trade-off: This provides fast, continuously updated features and separates stream processing from scoring, but introduces operational complexity and possible lag or inconsistency between Kafka processing and the Redis state.

values: Failure behavior: 25 ms timeout with rule-engine fallback
points.description: The service attempts its primary fraud score and permits it up to 25 ms. If the score is not returned within that limit, it applies the rule-engine fallback so a decision can still be produced. Trade-off: This provides bounded latency and continued operation, but sacrifices the primary scorer’s potentially richer or more accurate assessment whenever it times out; the 25 ms limit may therefore increase missed fraud or false declines.

values: Score audit record: append-only on-prem object store for 13 months
points.description: The service writes each fraud score and its audit information as new, non-modifiable entries in an on-premises object store. These records remain available for 13 months for retrospective review and auditing. Trade-off: This preserves a durable history and limits alteration of past scores, but prevents straightforward updates or deletions and creates on-premises storage and retention-management costs.

values: Training cadence: nightly Airflow on 90 days of labelled data
Model lineage: MLflow records runs and holds registry
Promotion gate: three-day shadow comparison and manual risk-team promotion
points.description: A nightly Airflow job trains a new model on 90 days of labelled data. Each run is recorded in MLflow and added to its registry, then the candidate runs in shadow mode for three days before the risk team manually promotes it. Trade-off: This provides regular retraining, reproducible lineage, and a cautious production gate, but the fixed 90-day window may limit historical context and manual approval slows deployment. The shadow period also postpones realizing a candidate model’s potential benefits.

values: Model type: neural network model
Serving runtime: Python REST on six autoscaling Kubernetes replicas
points.description: A neural network would compute a fraud score for each request, exposed through a Python REST service. Kubernetes would run six replicas of that service and autoscale them as request volume changes. Trade-off: This combines the neural network’s ability to model complex patterns with horizontally scalable service capacity and availability. It gives up some interpretability and incurs neural-network inference, Python/REST, and Kubernetes operational overhead, with potentially variable resource use as replicas scale.

values: Promotion gate: automated promotion after shadow comparison
points.description: 1. A new fraud-scoring model runs in shadow alongside the current scorer, producing scores without affecting live decisions. After comparing their results, the service automatically promotes the candidate when the comparison meets the gate. 2. Trade-off: This speeds releases and makes promotion consistent, but gives up a manual review checkpoint and may promote a model whose weaknesses the shadow comparison did not expose.

values: Activation: load promoted model without restarting the service
points.description: The service loads a newly promoted fraud-scoring model into memory while continuing to process requests. Once loaded, it switches scoring to the new model without restarting the service. Trade-off: This enables faster model deployment and avoids restart-related downtime. It adds runtime model-management complexity and can risk inconsistent scoring during the transition if requests overlap the switch.

alternatives.name: Fraud scoring as built
alternatives.summary: A Kafka and Flink feature path feeds a synchronous XGBoost scorer with a rule fallback. Scores and training lineage are retained, while nightly retraining is guarded by a three-day shadow review.

choices.value_id: Activity state: Kafka to Flink aggregates in Redis
choices.reason: Recent aggregates are called for, but Kafka, Flink and Redis are implementation choices; peak p99 is unproven.
choices.solution_quote: Flink jobs consume the topic and keep per-card aggregates (spend and counts over the last hour, day and week, and the number of distinct merchants) up to date in a Redis cluster.

choices.value_id: Scoring runtime: XGBoost Python REST on six autoscaling Kubernetes replicas
choices.reason: The service must score in the PCI environment and meet the latency target, but the model family, REST interface and replica count are not forced by the requirements and no benchmark settles the fit.
choices.solution_quote: The model is a gradient-boosted tree model (XGBoost). It is packaged in a container with a small Python REST service and runs on the company's Kubernetes cluster, with six replicas and autoscaling on CPU.

choices.value_id: Failure behavior: 25 ms timeout with rule-engine fallback
choices.reason: A fallback that allows authorization to continue is required by Q2; the specific timeout and use of the existing rule engine are reasonable implementations of that forced behavior.
choices.solution_quote: The authorization switch calls the service synchronously with a 25 ms timeout. If the call times out or fails, the switch uses the existing rule engine for that transaction and logs that no score was used.

choices.value_id: Score audit record: append-only on-prem object store for 13 months
choices.reason: Keeping the model version and every input for 13 months inside the certified environment is required; append-only object storage is a free implementation choice within that requirement.
choices.solution_quote: Every score is written, with the model version and all input values, to an append-only table in the company's on-premises object store, kept for 13 months.

choices.value_id: Training cadence: nightly Airflow on 90 days of labelled data
choices.reason: Updates as labels arrive are required, but nightly orchestration and the 90-day window are choices. The cadence supports updates but does not cure the slower promotion gate.
choices.solution_quote: An Airflow pipeline retrains the model every night on the last 90 days of labelled transactions.

choices.value_id: Model lineage: MLflow records runs and holds registry
choices.reason: The recorded snapshot, parameters, metrics and artifact support audit and comparison; MLflow is a tool choice, not a requirement.
choices.solution_quote: MLflow records the parameters, the metrics, the training data snapshot and the model artifact of every run, and holds the model registry.

choices.value_id: Promotion gate: three-day shadow comparison and manual risk-team promotion
choices.reason: Comparison before promotion is required, but manual promotion is not. The chosen three-day period directly exceeds Q4's 48-hour limit, so this choice is not justified by the stated target.
choices.solution_quote: A new model first runs in shadow mode next to the production model for three days; the risk team reviews the comparison and promotes it by hand in MLflow.

choices.value_id: Activation: load promoted model at service restart
choices.reason: Q4 constrains time to production but does not require restart-based loading. No restart duration is provided to establish that this choice meets the target.
choices.solution_quote: The scoring service loads the promoted model at its next restart.

choices.value_id: Score explanation: return three top features
choices.reason: Returning influential features helps explain declines, but Q3 asks for the exact input values and model provenance, not a ranked feature summary; this is an additional freely chosen aid.
choices.solution_quote: The service returns, with every score, the three features that pushed the score up the most, which the dispute team uses to explain declines to cardholders.

choices.value_id: Operations monitoring: Grafana distribution, fallback and drift dashboards/alerts
choices.reason: Monitoring gives operators signals about fallback and drift, but the chosen dashboard and alerting setup is not specified by a requirement.
choices.solution_quote: Grafana dashboards show the score distribution and the share of rule-engine fallbacks, and alert when the score distribution drifts from last month's.

adrs.title: Maintain recent card activity for online scoring
adrs.context: Scoring must use recent per-card activity within a tight request budget, and card data must remain in the certified environment. The implementation also needs to fit a small team without a dedicated ML platform group.

options.name: Kafka, Flink and Redis aggregates with XGBoost service
values: Activity state: Kafka to Flink aggregates in Redis
Scoring runtime: XGBoost Python REST on six autoscaling Kubernetes replicas
pros: Maintains rolling card aggregates for the request path.
Runs in the company's environment and can scale serving replicas.
cons: No peak p99 or capacity result demonstrates Q1.
options.reason: This combination is plausible for low-latency online features and is compatible with C1 when deployed inside the environment. The requirements do not force Kafka, Flink, Redis, XGBoost or six replicas; those choices remain unproven against Q1 and partly at odds with C2.

adrs.title: Retain enough evidence to reconstruct a score

Connects model artifacts to their training data snapshots.
cons: Specific storage and tracking products are choices.
options.reason: The retention, fields and in-environment location are forced by R3, Q3 and C1. Append-only object storage and MLflow are free implementation choices that provide the needed records.

adrs.title: Retrain and control model promotion
adrs.context: Delayed confirmed labels require recurring retraining, with lineage for audit and a comparison against the current model before release. A release must reach production within 48 hours under Q4.
